name: Energy medicine

card.summary: A group of healing practices, such as Reiki and biofield therapy, based on the belief that a body energy field can be balanced; people use it for relaxation and stress relief that some link to how they look.
card.note: Reviews report no evidence of clinical efficacy; harm arises mainly when it replaces medical treatment.

quick.overview:
Energy medicine covers practices in which healers claim to channel or rebalance a body energy field, hands-on, hands-off or at a distance. Reiki, therapeutic touch, qigong and crystal healing are typical examples.

In appearance culture, its pull is relaxation and stress reduction, which practitioners connect to skin, sleep and general glow. Research reviews, however, have not found clinical efficacy for energy healing.
quick.how: Sessions are usually a practitioner holding hands near or on the body, or distance healing. Some people use qigong self-practice. It is generally used alongside everyday care.
quick.risks: The main documented harm is delaying or forgoing medical treatment. Some device sellers have been prosecuted by the FDA for false claims.

lead: Energy medicine is a branch of alternative medicine built on the belief that healers can direct healing energy into patients. Wikipedia describes it as pseudoscientific and notes the concept is unrelated to the physical concept of energy [1]. Practitioners work hands-on, hands-off or at a distance [1].

Main forms include biofield healing, therapeutic touch, Reiki, qigong, crystal healing and Pranic Healing [1]. The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health divides the field into veritable energy medicine (measurable energies like magnets and light) and putative energy medicine (energies that cannot be measured, such as Reiki) [1].

Proponents hold that illness reflects imbalance in the body's energy field and that rebalancing restores wellbeing [1]. In appearance and wellness culture the draw is relaxation: advocates link calm and lower stress to better sleep, skin and a rested look, a connection that belongs to practitioners' beliefs rather than to tested outcomes. Reviews summarised by Wikipedia and statements from NCCIH report that the research is limited in quality and that no clinical efficacy has been established, while NCCIH reports that Reiki has not been shown to have harmful effects [1][5].

chain: Sleep and skin often tied to stress
angle.text: Users seek relaxation and stress relief, which some connect to better sleep and fresher-looking skin. The link to appearance is a belief held by practitioners, not an outcome tested in trials.

infobox: Reiki, therapeutic touch, qigong, biofield healing, distant healing [1]
About $40 to $300 per Reiki session in US hospitals (2014 report) [3]
No US regulation of Reiki practitioners; FDA regulates some devices [1][3]

paras: In the 19th century, electricity and magnetism spread widely as health claims, and in the early 20th century radioactive materials were marketed similarly; more recently quantum mechanics has been used in the same way [1]. The term 'energy medicine' has been in general use since the International Society for the Study of Subtle Energies and Energy Medicine was founded in the 1980s [1]. Bioresonance therapy was invented in Germany in 1977 by Franz Morell and Erich Rasche, and in 2005-2006 the North American Nursing Diagnosis Association approved an 'energy field disturbance' diagnosis, which was strongly criticised [1].

Reiki was created in Japan in the 1920s by Mikao Usui, who died in 1926. His disciple Chujiro Hayashi taught it, and Hawayo Takata, Hayashi's student, started the first US Reiki clinic in 1970 [3]. Practitioners place their palms on or near the body, or work at a distance, and describe a 'universal energy' flowing to the client; sessions typically last about an hour [3]. A 2014 Washington Post report found at least 60 US hospitals offering it at $40 to $300 per session, and Cancer Research UK reported in 2019 that some UK cancer centres and hospices offered it free or at low cost [3]. No central authority controls the term, and certificates can be bought online [3]. NCCIH describes Reiki as a complementary approach in which practitioners lightly touch or hover over a person to support the body's natural healing [5].

Therapeutic touch was developed in the 1970s by Dolores Krieger, later a professor of nursing at New York University, and Dora Kunz, who led the Theosophical Society in America from 1975 to 1987; practitioners claim to sense and manipulate a patient's energy field with their hands on or near the body [4]. Alan Sokal's 2006 estimate counted more than 80 colleges and universities in about 70 countries teaching it and roughly 80 North American hospitals practising it [4]. In April 1998 JAMA published an experiment designed by nine-year-old Emily Rosa in which 21 practitioners tried to locate her hovering hand behind a screen; they were correct 44 percent of the time [4].

Qigong combines posture, movement, breathing and meditation intended to cultivate and balance qi, and is practised worldwide for exercise, relaxation and meditation [6]. Its roots go back more than 2,000 years, the term was promoted in the late 1940s and 1950s, and by the 1990s there were estimated to be 60 to 200 million practitioners in China [6]. In 1999 the Chinese government cracked down on public qigong practice and banned groups including Falun Gong, and since then qigong has been officially supported in the context of health and traditional medicine [6]. Wikipedia reports that only limited numbers of studies meet randomised-trial standards, that reviews of pain, cancer and cardiovascular conditions have called the evidence inconclusive, and that a 2026 British Journal of Sports Medicine umbrella review of traditional Chinese exercises reported high-certainty evidence for some benefits, such as physical function in knee osteoarthritis and sleep quality in fibromyalgia [6]. Qigong is generally viewed as safe, with cautions similar to other physical activity [6].

Wikipedia also describes polarity therapy, founded by Randolph Stone; earthing, promoted by the Earthing Institute through direct contact with the ground; and bioresonance devices, some of which use skin-resistance measurement [1]. The FDA classifies resistance-measurement diagnostic devices as Class III and has banned some and prosecuted sellers for false claims [1].

Schools of energy healing include biofield healing, spiritual healing, contact and distant healing, Pranic Healing, therapeutic touch, Reiki and qigong [1]. Proponents say imbalances in the body's energy field cause illness and that rebalancing restores health; some modalities describe symptoms after treatment as a 'release' [1].

Proposed explanations include quantum non-locality for distant healing, bioelectromagnetism, James Oschman's 1997 account of healer-sourced electromagnetic fields, and Beverly Rubik's 2002 biofield hypothesis drawing on systems and chaos theory [1][7]. Critics call these ideas pseudophysics, and even supporters acknowledge that the theoretical foundations are tenuous [1]. One review defined the biofield as including nonclassical and quantum energy fields [7]. NCCIH states that there is no scientific evidence supporting the existence of the energy field thought to play a role in Reiki [5].

A 2000 systematic review of 23 distant-healing trials by Astin and colleagues was inconclusive because of methodological problems, and a 2001 randomised trial of 120 chronic-pain patients by Abbot and colleagues found no efficacy for either distance or face-to-face healing. Edzard Ernst concluded in 2003 and 2006 that the evidence had turned negative, and a 2014 trial in colorectal cancer patients showed no improvement in quality of life, depression, mood or sleep [1].

A 2008 systematic review by Lee, Pittler and Ernst of nine randomised Reiki trials found widespread methodological flaws and concluded the value of Reiki remained unproven [3]. NCCIH states that most Reiki research is not high quality and its results are inconsistent, and that Reiki has not been clearly shown to be effective for any health-related purpose; its page was last updated in December 2018 [5].

Other trials cover Reiki for fibromyalgia, therapeutic touch for procedural pain in very preterm neonates (titled 'not therapeutic'), a Jin Shin Jyutsu treatment study in women with breast cancer and a pilot energy-medicine study for chronic headaches [8][9][10][11]. A randomised double-blind trial of Spiritist 'passe' healing in preterm newborns examined stress hormone, pain and length of stay [2]. A review of pilot studies with cultured cells tested whether practitioners could perceive a biofield [12]. A 1998 JAMA trial of therapeutic touch practitioners found 44 percent correct detection, and a 2004 Cochrane review of therapeutic touch for wounds was withdrawn in 2016 over concerns about the included studies [4].

Reliance on energy healing has been linked to serious harm or death when patients delay medical treatment [1]. Safety risks of Reiki itself are considered very low; the main concern is replacing proven treatments for serious conditions [3]. The FDA classifies devices that diagnose and treat disease by resistance measurements as Class III, has banned some, and has prosecuted sellers for false claims [1]. The Oregon Board of Chiropractic Examiners barred chiropractors from using the EPFX device [1].

Reported improvements are generally attributed by reviewers to placebo effects, spontaneous remission and research flaws such as lack of blinding and publication bias [1]. Critics such as Stephen Barrett of Quackwatch and David Gorski have been strongly critical of Reiki, and the US Conference of Catholic Bishops issued 2009 guidelines saying Reiki lacks scientific support and is incompatible with Christian teaching [3]. The American Academy of Neurology and partner bodies advised against considering Reiki for painful diabetic neuropathy [3]. A study of news coverage of complementary and alternative medicine examined how media report on such therapies [13].

Energy medicine sits at the edge of appearance culture: its practices are offered for relaxation, sleep and stress reduction, and wellness writers connect those with skin and a rested look. Dedicated discussion in looksmaxxing forums is sparse; the claims come mainly from the wellness and alternative-medicine world.

lore.intro: Claims about energy medicine come mainly from practitioners, wellness writers and alternative-medicine organisations rather than looksmaxxing forums; the claims below are those most often made [1][3][5].

claims.claim: Rebalancing the body's energy field restores health and wellbeing
claims.believers: Practitioners hold that illness reflects an imbalance in the energy field and that hands-on or distance sessions rebalance it [1].
claims.experts: Reviews report no evidence supporting clinical use, and NCCIH states there is no scientific evidence for the energy field thought to be involved in Reiki [1][5].

claims.claim: Reiki relaxes people and lowers stress and anxiety
claims.believers: Users describe calm and relief during and after sessions, and some physicians suggest it may support general wellbeing [3].
claims.experts: A 2008 review of nine trials found flaws and called the value unproven; NCCIH says results are inconsistent, and Reiki has not been shown to cause harm [3][5].

claims.claim: Practitioners can sense a person's biofield
claims.believers: Therapeutic touch teachers say practitioners can feel the field by hand near the body [4].
claims.experts: In Emily Rosa's 1998 JAMA experiment, 21 practitioners located a hand 44 percent of the time, within the range of chance; pilot work with cultured cells also tested biofield perception [4][12].

claims.claim: Healing can be sent at a distance
claims.believers: Some proponents invoke quantum non-locality to explain distant healing [1].
claims.experts: A 2000 review was inconclusive, a 2001 trial of 120 chronic-pain patients found no efficacy, and Ernst judged the evidence negative in 2003 and 2006; critics call the physics explanations pseudophysics [1].

claims.believers: Practitioners and Chinese health bodies promote it for exercise, relaxation and prevention [6].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports few trials meeting randomised standards, inconclusive reviews for several conditions and a 2026 umbrella review reporting high-certainty benefits for some outcomes such as knee osteoarthritis function and fibromyalgia sleep; it is generally viewed as safe [6].

claims.claim: Energy devices can diagnose and treat disease
claims.believers: Sellers of bioresonance and similar devices claim to detect disease and addictions through energy measurements [1].
claims.experts: The FDA classifies resistance-measurement diagnostic devices as Class III, has banned some and prosecuted sellers for false claims; studies such as Schöni 1997 found no effect beyond placebo [1].

claims.claim: Energy healing can replace conventional treatment
claims.believers: Some practitioners present it as treatment without drugs [1].
claims.experts: Reliance on spiritual or energetic healing has been linked to serious harm or death when patients delay or forgo treatment [1][3].
